form: 4 Salish lexical considerations

Affixation (and reduplication) occur freely across not just verbs but also nouns and adjectives, historically taken as proof that distinctions between Salishan (e.g. noun and verb) morphemes were meaningless. Modern interpretations, resulting from lexical testing, have identified lexical categories in many Salishan languages: Okanagan (Hébert, 1983) and ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Comox-Sliammon) (Huijsmans, 2023), to name two. The universality of verb, noun and adjective distinctions does appear to be meaningful in Salishan languages, albeit more weakly than for languages outside the Pacific Northwest.

form: 4.1 Morphology and syntax

From the universe of academic typological research on Salish, three features are briefly noted: lexical affixation; the role of (2P) clitics; cognates across Salish family languages. The statistics underlying the following categories are exposed in the UD treebank pages for each language: POS tags used, features and relations. Corpus morphology and syntax are also exposed, providing helpful summaries for the annotated data.

form: 4.1.1 Affixation

In agglutinative languages (Ikonnikova et al., 2024), morphemes are segmentable and attached around a definable root to form a word, with affixes (prefixes, suffixes) typically mapping to a single morphological/ syntactic form — a one-to-one mapping. Agglutinative language affixes mark syntactic features on a root or noun. Cases are important and feature successfully in many UD annotations.

form: Diachronic cognates across lexical suffixes and clitic/affixal person markers are evidence for a shared annotation schema and a common lexical-suffix inventory to span the 23 Salish languages.
